newsitem.title: USA: White House in tentative Alaska lumber deal.
newsitem.headline: White House in tentative Alaska lumber deal.

text.p: Alaska Sen. Frank Murkowski said Thursday the White House tentatively agreed to keep a transition supply of lumber flowing to two Southeast Alaska sawmills in an effort to break a stalemate over a national parks bill.
"The current reality is that this is not a done deal," Murkowski, a Republican, said at a news conference.
But he had a letter initialed by White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta to release lumber that was to go to the Ketchikan Pulp Mill to be available instead for two Ketchikan company sawmills.
The letter called for mutually cancelling the U.S. Forest Service's contract with Louisiana-Pacific Corp's Ketchikan Pulp Mill, that the company planned to close soon.
Timber from the Tongass National Forest under contract to the pulp mill -- about 300 million board feet or a two-year supply for two Southeast Alaska sawmills -- would be released.
Murkowski had insisted on some provision to keep a timber supply to the sawmills before removing a hold on the national parks bill.
"We were successful in resolving how there would be some supply to the sawmills," Murkowski said.
He said the timber deal did not change the parks bill. Once the White House officially signed off on the letter, he said the Senate would vote on the parks bill the House passed Saturday.
The Senate -- slated to adjourn for the year later Thursday -- was to pass the parks bill on a voice vote.
Since the Senate bill was identical to the House's, the bill would be ready for President Clinton's expected signature.
"This bill will pass, it will go to the president, and he will sign it," Murkowski said.
